opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea of that paper, as I understand it, is that individual benchmarks are terrible for measuring long-run trends. Each one saturates within a year or two, they're on arbitrary scales, and you can't directly compare a score on one with a score on another. The Rosetta Stone approach stitches them together. Because many models are evaluated on several overlapping benchmarks, you can fit a latent model, something like item response theory, where each model gets a single capability score and each benchmark gets a difficulty and a slope. Then you have one continuous scale that runs across many generations of models, even as particular benchmarks come and go.

If you're worried about an intelligence explosion, that's exactly the instrument you want, because what you're looking for isn't "capabilities are high," it's "the rate of improvement is itself increasing." With a stitched scale you can plot capability against time and ask whether the trend is linear on that scale, which you could read as steady exponential progress in underlying inputs, or whether it's bending upward. A sustained, superexponential kink, particularly one not explained by a known jump in compute or spending, is the signature you'd watch for.

There are a few refinements I'd add. First, control for inputs. Plot capability against training compute as well as calendar time. If capability per unit of compute is accelerating, that suggests algorithmic progress is speeding up, which is the channel through which AI automating AI research would show up first. Second, weight the benchmarks that matter. You can build a sub-scale specifically from AI R&D-relevant tasks, like coding, ML engineering, and long-horizon agentic work, and see whether that dimension is pulling away from general knowledge benchmarks. Third, treat it as an early-warning system and set thresholds in advance, so you're not rationalizing after the fact.

Then the caveats, which are real. Contamination and benchmark gaming can produce fake acceleration. The stitching relies on assumptions, like a single latent dimension, that get shakier as models become more lopsided. Benchmarks are a lagging and noisy proxy for actual research productivity, so I'd want to triangulate with things like internal lab measurements of how much AI is speeding up their researchers. And the newest, most informative frontier is where you have the fewest overlapping data points, so your error bars are widest exactly where you care most.

So it won't tell you on its own that an intelligence explosion is happening. But it's one of the better tools we have for turning a vague sense that things are speeding up into something you can measure and argue about.

r001.rationale: It says overlapping benchmarks can be stitched into a continuous capability scale across model generations, even as individual benchmarks saturate and come and go.

r002.rationale: It proposes checking whether capability trends are linear or bend upward, but does not state that observed general capability scores so far have followed an approximately linear trend against model release dates.

r003.rationale: It proposes plotting capability over time and watching for a sustained upward bend or superexponential kink as a signature of an emerging intelligence explosion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core idea of the Rosetta Stone paper, as I understand it, is that benchmarks are all measuring on different scales, and the trick is to put them on a common footing. You take a bunch of models, run them on a bunch of benchmarks, and then fit something like an item response model, so that each benchmark gets translated into a shared latent "capability" axis. Then a score of 60% on one eval and 40% on another can actually be compared, because you've learned how each one maps onto that underlying scale. And crucially, when a benchmark saturates and everyone moves on to a harder one, you don't lose continuity, because the new benchmark gets stitched onto the same scale.

So if I wanted to use that to look for an intelligence explosion, the thing I'd really care about isn't the level of capability, it's the second derivative. The basic story of an intelligence explosion is that AI starts contributing to AI research, that speeds up progress, which makes better AI, and so on. The signature of that in the data should be that the rate of capability gain per unit of calendar time starts bending upward, and ideally bending upward faster than you'd predict from just compute scaling and the normal algorithmic progress trend.

Right now that's really hard to see, because each benchmark only gives you a window of a year or two before it's saturated, and you can't tell whether the curve across benchmarks is accelerating or whether you just switched to a harder test with a different scale. The Rosetta Stone approach is exactly what you'd want to fix that. You get one long time series on a common axis, going back several years, and you can actually ask: is this trend linear in the latent variable, or is it curving?

Then there are a few refinements I'd want. The first is that I wouldn't look at general capability. I'd look specifically at the subset of benchmarks that measure AI R&D-relevant skills: things like ML engineering tasks, research replication, long-horizon agentic coding, the METR-style time-horizon measurements. Those are the capabilities that feed back into the loop. If general capability is going up smoothly but AI R&D capability is bending upward faster, that's a much more worrying signal than the reverse.

The second thing is that you'd want to control for inputs. An upward bend in capability per calendar month could just be that people are spending much more on compute. So I'd try to plot capability against training compute, or against effective compute, and look at whether the capability you get per unit of compute is itself accelerating. That residual, the algorithmic efficiency gain, is the thing that AI automating research should actually move.

And the third thing, honestly, is that I'd combine it with more direct measurements, because benchmarks are a lagging and noisy proxy. If you're inside a lab, you can just ask: what fraction of the research engineering work is being done by AI systems, and what's the measured speedup? The Rosetta Stone approach is most valuable for people outside the labs, or for cross-lab comparison, where you only have access to the public evals.

The caveat I'd give is that I'm somewhat skeptical you'll get a clean early-warning signal out of this. The whole worry about intelligence explosions is that the transition could be fast relative to the time it takes to run evals, publish results, and fit the model. So I'd treat this as a way to confirm or rule out the slower versions of the story, where things accelerate over months to a couple of years. For the really fast versions, you'd want things that are much more real-time, like monitoring inside labs. But even confirming that we're on the slow path, or on no path at all, would be genuinely useful for how much we should be panicking.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark saturation limits each eval to a short window, and that stitching benchmarks onto a shared scale enables a continuous time series spanning several years.

r002.rationale: It asks whether the capability trend is linear or curving, but never states that scores so far have followed an approximately linear trend against model release dates.

r003.rationale: It proposes looking for accelerating capability gains over time, but explicitly says it would not look at general capability and instead focuses on AI R&D relevant skills.

astra-6.text:
I’d try to use it to measure the capabilities that feed back into AI development. The basic idea is to put different benchmarks onto a common scale, so that you can track progress even as individual benchmarks saturate and get replaced.

For an intelligence explosion, the interesting question isn’t just whether AI is getting better at answering questions. It’s whether AI is getting better at doing AI research, and whether that improvement is causing the next round of progress to happen faster. So I’d want measurements of things like designing experiments, debugging training runs, and coming up with useful algorithmic improvements. Ideally, you’d measure how much those capabilities actually speed up a research team.

Then you could look for a feedback loop: better AI systems lead to faster AI research, which produces better systems, which accelerate research further. You’d also want to track the resources going into that process. If progress speeds up because we’ve dramatically increased spending on compute, that’s different evidence from progress speeding up because AI is making research more productive.

The benchmark approach could help make the capability trend interpretable. But an accelerating capability curve alone wouldn’t establish an intelligence explosion. You’d need evidence that the acceleration is being driven by that feedback loop.

r001.rationale: It says to put different benchmarks on a common scale so progress can be tracked as individual benchmarks saturate and are replaced.

r002.rationale: It does not state that benchmark-derived general capability scores have followed an approximately linear trend against model release dates.

r003.rationale: It discusses an accelerating capability curve and feedback loop, but does not specifically propose checking for acceleration in benchmark-derived general capability scores over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d try to use it to get a more consistent measure of how capabilities are improving. One problem with looking at individual benchmarks is that their scores aren’t particularly comparable: a ten-percentage-point improvement on one benchmark might represent a much bigger change than the same improvement on another. And benchmarks saturate, so you’re constantly switching to new ones.

The Rosetta Stone approach is to use the overlap between models evaluated on different benchmarks to put those results onto a common scale. You could then ask how that underlying capability measure changes with training compute, and how it changes over time.

For an intelligence explosion, though, the thing I’d particularly want to track is the ability to do AI research. Are models becoming better at designing experiments, writing the code, interpreting results, and coming up with useful new ideas? And does deploying those models actually make the next round of AI development faster?

You’d be looking for that feedback loop: better AI leads to faster AI research, which leads to better AI. An acceleration in the benchmark-derived measure would be a useful signal, but it wouldn’t by itself establish that this feedback loop was responsible. You’d want to connect it to evidence about how AI research is actually being done.

r001.rationale: It says benchmark scores can be placed on a common scale using overlap between models, while noting that benchmarks saturate and must be replaced, enabling the underlying capability measure to be tracked over time.

r002.rationale: It asks how capability changes over time but does not state that scores have followed an approximately linear trend against model release dates.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says acceleration in the benchmark-derived measure would be a useful signal of an intelligence explosion.
